title: The Locker-Room Smell
briefing: Jordan, 13, walks into the team locker room after a hot practice and nearly gags at the smell. Ten minutes later he's laughing with teammates and can't smell a thing. Then his friend walks in late and shouts, “How can you guys stand it in here?”
question: Did the smell go away — or did Jordan's nose stop telling him about it?

clues.title: Awful at the door
clues.text: The moment he opens the door the smell hits him hard. He pulls his shirt over his nose.
clues.shows: a strong new smell being noticed straight away

clues.title: Gone in ten minutes
clues.text: Ten minutes later he honestly can't smell anything. He even forgets it was bad.
clues.shows: how strongly he notices the smell dropping over time

clues.title: The late friend
clues.text: His friend arrives fifteen minutes late and is disgusted. Nobody has opened a window or cleaned anything.
clues.shows: that the smell is still in the air at full strength

clues.title: Back in after a break
clues.text: Jordan steps outside for five minutes to grab his water bottle. When he walks back in, the smell hits him again.
clues.shows: noticing coming back after a break from the smell

hypotheses.text: The smell faded away on its own, or someone aired out the room.
hypotheses.flaw: His friend smelled it at full strength fifteen minutes later, and nobody opened a window — the smell was still there.

hypotheses.text: Jordan just stopped paying attention because he was busy talking.
hypotheses.flaw: Coming back from outside, he was still busy and still not trying to notice — yet the smell hit him again. Something in his nose had reset.

hypotheses.text: Smell receptors in his nose fire hard at a new smell but quiet down when it doesn't change, so his brain stops getting the alarm — even though the smell is still in the air.
The strong smell damaged his nose so it stopped working.
hypotheses.flaw: A damaged nose would not recover in five minutes outside — but his sense of smell came straight back.

prediction.prompt: Jordan stays in the locker room for twenty minutes. How strongly does he notice the smell as the minutes go by?

second.question: And the amount of smell actually in the air during those twenty minutes?

concepts.label: smell receptors
concepts.hint: What in his nose actually detects the smell?

concepts.label: they adapt to a steady smell
concepts.hint: What happens to those detectors when the smell doesn't change?

concepts.label: the smell is still there
concepts.hint: What did the late friend prove about the room?

concepts.label: the brain stops getting the alarm
concepts.hint: Where does the message 'bad smell!' end up?

concepts.label: a break resets it
concepts.hint: Why did the smell hit him again after five minutes outside?

transfer.context: Hana, 14, puts on perfume before school. By lunch she can't smell it at all and thinks it has worn off — but her friend sitting next to her says she can still smell it clearly.
options: Perfume only works on other people's noses.
Hana's smell receptors adapted to the steady smell, so her brain stopped reporting it — her friend's nose hasn't adapted.
transfer.retryHint: Someone else can still smell it — which of Jordan's clues showed exactly that?
transfer.explanation: The perfume is still there, just like the locker-room smell. Hana's receptors have been smelling it all morning and have quieted down, while her friend's nose is meeting it fresh. Senses report change, not sameness.

takeaway: Your senses report change, not sameness. Smell receptors quiet down when a smell stays the same, so you stop noticing it — even though it never left. A short break resets them.
